source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Difficulty of one-move matchstick problems follows how wide the constraint is that must be relaxed: value changes (Type A) easiest, operator changes (B) harder, tautology (C) hardest. Tight-chunk decomposition (D) is harder than loose-chunk (A).
numbers: Exp 1A, N=20 (German students, 5 min limit): problem type effect F(3,57)=7.11, p<.001; order C<B<A and A<D (A vs D p<.05). Type D solved 75% in block 1 and 90% in block 2.
limits: Small N. Type B near ceiling in some experiments (over 80% in Exp 2), so the A vs B gap is not always significant. Roman-numeral domain only.
agent_relevance: O4 should target the widest hidden constraint; the hardest ones are those the solver treats as part of what the task means. An O4 prompt could ask which assumptions feel like part of the definition.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Exp 1B and Exp 2 repeated the problem-type ordering in new samples, including US students (Exp 2, N=78). In Exp 2, similarity of numerals or order between blocks did not change transfer.
numbers: Exp 1B N=38 (between-subject versions). Exp 2 mean solved: Block 1 66%, Block 2 96%. Block 1 by condition: same-same 67, same-order 64, same-numerals 64, different-different 71. Similarity effect F(3,74)=0.34 (n.s.).
limits: Authors report ceiling effects for Types A and B. Transfer was clearest for the hard problem types.
agent_relevance: Practice on a problem that needed a given constraint dropped helps on others needing the same one, even when they look different. Supports storing which constraint was dropped as a reusable note, not the surface problem.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Exp 3 used the tautology form. Prior exposure to tautological problems did not change how hard the tight-chunk Type D problems were, consistent with chunk tightness (not equation form) driving difficulty.
numbers: Exp 3: Type D solved 61% (regular-first, N=18) vs 69% (tautology-first, N=16) in Block 1, chi2(1,N=34)=0.22, p=.64. Block 2: 92% vs 94%. Type A 94% and 97%. Type C could not be compared (all solved).
limits: Ceiling effects prevented some predicted tests. Small groups.
agent_relevance: Chunk decomposition (splitting a unit the solver treats as atomic) is a different operator from constraint relaxation. O6 needs a split the unit prompt, not only reframe.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson & Raney (2001) An eye movement study of insight problem solving
finding: Eye-movement study. Problem B (constraint relaxation) and C (tight chunk) were solved less often than A (loose chunk). Mean fixation duration was higher for B and C than A and grew over the trial, which fits an impasse.
numbers: N=24, 5 min limit. Solved: A 23/24, B 9/24 (chi2(1,N=24)=18.38, p<.001 vs A), C 18/24 (chi2=4.18, p<.05 vs A); B vs C chi2=4.78, p<.05. Fixation duration: problem effect F(2,44)=3.49, p<.05; interval effect F(2,44)=8.58, p<.001.
limits: One lab, N=24, one domain. Fixations split by median into short and long.
agent_relevance: A measurable trace of a wrong frame: attention stays on values until the frame changes. The agent can watch whether its candidates keep touching the same elements.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson & Raney (2001) An eye movement study of insight problem solving
finding: Predicted shift in attention after restructuring: in successful trials the share of long-fixation time on the crucial element rises late. Unsuccessful trials show no such shift.
numbers: Success by interval interactions F(1,22)=7.91, p<.01 and F(2,42)=5.08, p<.05 (long fixations); main effect of success F(1,21)=3.09, p=.09 (n.s.). Chance share per element 20% of fixation time.
limits: Modest interactions, post hoc three-interval split.
agent_relevance: Supports a testable signal for frame changed: a sudden move of focus to a previously ignored part.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson & Raney (2001) An eye movement study of insight problem solving
finding: Rival accounts named in the paper: Gestalt restructuring, progress monitoring, and search with heuristics. The authors argue only representational change fits both solution-rate and eye-movement data, and that the others explain single findings.
numbers: Three predictions tested at N=24: impasse lengthens fixations; early attention goes to values; later attention goes to the relevant chunk in solvers.
limits: The only theory that explains all claim is the authors own. Later work (Jones 2003, Fedor 2015) gives mixed support.
agent_relevance: Treat the theory as a good engineering guide for operators, not a settled account of mechanism.

source: Graf et al. (2023) Tracing cognitive processes in insight problem solving: GAMs and change point analysis
finding: Re-analysis of whether insight is sudden. Linear models miss a shift; only nonlinear models (GAM, change-point) detect an abrupt burst of attention to the critical element (the plus sign) late in solving. Change point near the 90% time bin.
numbers: N=61 (mean age 22.8). Only 34% solved within 5 min; another 11% after the hint You can change the operators, too (45% total).
limits: Single hard problem. Time bins are proportional to each persons total time. Claims of suddenness depend on the model used.
agent_relevance: Suddenness may depend on the metric. Track restructuring as an abrupt change in what the agent attends to, and do not read slow progress as a frame shift.

source: Graf et al. (2023) Tracing cognitive processes in insight problem solving: GAMs and change point analysis
finding: Explicit hint effects: after a hint to change operators, non-solvers showed an immediate burst of attention to plus and equals that faded, while later solvers built up attention gradually. The hint moved attention for everyone, but only helped some.
numbers: Attention on equals about doubled right after the hint. Attention on plus rose only 4% at first and doubled by the 20% bin. 11 percentage points of the sample solved after the hint.
limits: Only non-solvers received the hint, so groups are not randomized. No hint-less control for extra time.
agent_relevance: A hint that names the constraint (O4 prompt) redirects attention, but many stuck solvers still fail. Follow O4 with a check that the candidate really uses the dropped constraint.

source: Graf et al. (2023) Tracing cognitive processes in insight problem solving: GAMs and change point analysis
finding: Method warning: the same data analysed with ANOVA on 10 time bins hid the abrupt shift that GAM and change-point models found.
numbers: GAM and change-point (MCP) models both found a late shift; MCP put it near the 90% bin; linear analysis placed it differently.
limits: Individual-level change points not shown in the text read.
agent_relevance: Benchmark traces for the agent should use change-point analysis per item, not averages.

source: Nasvytis et al. (2026) Leveraging speech to identify signatures of insight and transfer in problem solving (CogSci)
finding: Online think-aloud matchstick study. Problem types ordered as in 1999: value-loose-chunk easiest, tautological hardest. Repeating the same problem type across 5 trials sharply improved accuracy; mixing types did not.
numbers: N=189, 4 min per trial. Value-loose-chunk 80.7% correct, tautological 19.2%. Same-type group accuracy 0.32 on trial 1 to 0.75 on trial 5; Different group stayed in a narrow band.
limits: Online sample, automatic speech transcription, LLM (GPT-5.1) labels. Conference paper.
agent_relevance: A large-N replication (about 9 times Knoblich 1999 Exp 1A) of the constraint-scope difficulty order. Transfer needs the same abstract change type.

source: Nasvytis et al. (2026) Leveraging speech to identify signatures of insight and transfer in problem solving (CogSci)
finding: What people say changes at first success: they speak more, consider fewer distinct candidate moves, and talk about different things. After success they start naming the problem type, but only when the same type keeps repeating.
numbers: Categorisation utterances rose from 0.3% at first success to 2.1% post-success (about 7 times), +1.8 percentage points, 95% CI [.007,.030]. Distinct candidate moves fell by 2.11 (Same) and 2.24 (Different) at first success vs before, CIs exclude 0.
limits: Classifier accuracy for first-success vs pre-success about .64, modest. Correlational.
agent_relevance: Naming the type of change seems to make a restructuring reusable. The agent should write down the type of change after success (an O6 note), not just the answer.

source: Kershaw & Ohlsson (2001) Training for insight: the case of the nine-dot problem (CogSci)
finding: Training on easy problems that required turning at non-dot points raised solving of a nine-dot variant. Opposite training did not push performance below control.
numbers: N=90, 30 per group. First insight problem solved: facilitating 19/30 (63%), hindering 8/30 (27%), none 11/30 (37%). chi2(2,N=90)=8.836, p<.05. Facilitating vs none chi2(1,N=60)=4.267, p<.05; hindering vs none n.s. (0.693). Mean time 116 s facilitating, 188 s hindering. Those who completed training correctly: 17/19 (89%) solved vs 2/11 (18%).
limits: Conference paper. The hindering null is probably a floor effect (nine-dot baseline under 5% in minutes, as cited). Participants who completed training were self-selected by performance.
agent_relevance: Direct intervention with a 26 point gain over control: pre-solving easy items that break the same constraint helps. A warm-up of that kind may help the agent.

source: Kershaw & Ohlsson (2001) Training for insight: the case of the nine-dot problem (CogSci)
finding: Older tests of the Gestalt account (cited second-hand): telling people they may go outside the square helped only when combined with hints that gave away part of the solution.
numbers: Burnham & Davis 1969 and Weisberg & Alba 1981, as cited in the paper. Nine-dot solving under 5% in a few minutes (Lung & Dominowski 1985; MacGregor et al. 2001, as cited).
limits: Second-hand from the paper introduction.
agent_relevance: A bare drop-the-constraint prompt (O4) is weak. Pair it with a concrete start move or a worked analogy.

source: Kershaw & Ohlsson (2001) Training for insight: the case of the nine-dot problem (CogSci)
finding: Nine-dot variants that need turning on a non-dot point are harder than those that do not. This points to a narrower hidden constraint (turn only on dots) than the Gestalt stay-inside-the-square idea.
numbers: Reported in the paper discussion; no separate effect size read.
limits: Conference paper.
agent_relevance: The hidden constraint can be narrower than the obvious one. O4 prompts should ask for the narrowest assumption.

source: Fedor, Szathmary & Ollinger (2015) Problem solving stages in the five square problem
finding: Behavioural test of the four-stage insight model (search, impasse, insight, search) on the five-square matchstick problem. Most solvers did not follow the classic order. Search and impasse recurred several times.
numbers: N=129 online participants from 37 countries (42 control, 87 impasse-monitoring). Solution rate 51% (55% control, 49% monitoring); 39% after exclusions. Impasse button pressed by 33% of solvers vs 79% of non-solvers (monitoring group).
limits: Online, self-paced. Self-reported impasse did not rise during behaviourally defined impasse stages, so impasse reports are unreliable. The proposed model is post hoc.
agent_relevance: Plan for loops (stuck, reframe, stuck again) in the state machine; do not stop after the first reframe.

source: Fedor, Szathmary & Ollinger (2015) Problem solving stages in the five square problem
finding: Solvers explore more widely: non-solvers repeat positions more. Solvers also report insight more often than non-solvers.
numbers: Repetition rate non-solvers M=0.5 (SD=0.2) vs solvers M=0.3 (SD=0.3), t(99)=5.13, p<.0001. Insight reported by 74% of solvers (29/39) vs 10% of non-solvers (6/62).
limits: Subjective insight reports measure feeling, not restructuring.
agent_relevance: Repeated states are a cheap external stuck-detector for the agent.

source: Jones (2003) Testing two cognitive theories of insight (abstract via PubMed)
finding: Jones tested representational change against progress monitoring on an unlimited-move problem. Both theories got support, but manipulations of the problem favoured representational change as the better predictor.
numbers: Abstract only (PubMed); no numbers read.
limits: Abstract only. Rival theory (MacGregor, Ormerod & Chronicle 2001): insight is sought once distance to goal looks unachievable in the moves left. The two are not mutually exclusive.
agent_relevance: Two triggers for reframing exist: the frame seems wrong, and the budget will run out. Use both, but choose the operator by which constraint was assumed.

source: Ollinger, Jones, Faber & Knoblich (2013) Cognitive mechanisms of insight: eight-coin problem (abstract via PubMed)
finding: Eight-coin problem has two sources of difficulty: assuming the solution lies in 2-D (a constraint) and perceptual groupings (chunks). Move choice followed the established representation, not appropriate heuristics. Authors say this favours representational change over the move-availability account of Ormerod et al. (2002).
numbers: Six new problem versions; sample size not read (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only. Competing account: Ormerod, MacGregor & Chronicle (2002), version differences from which moves are available in 2-D search.
agent_relevance: The same two operators (drop a constraint, split a chunk) show up in a third problem type, so O4 and O6 are not limited to matchstick arithmetic.

source: Ollinger, Jones & Knoblich (2006) Heuristics and representational change in two-move matchstick tasks
finding: Two-move matchstick tasks: difficulty followed the amount of representational change required, while heuristics had minimal effect on solution rates.
numbers: 120 participants (from a search summary; not read in full).
limits: Not opened: PDF blocked. Secondary summary only.
agent_relevance: A good-sounding heuristic does not fix a wrong frame. Do not rely on generic search heuristics when the frame is wrong.

source: Ollinger, Jones & Knoblich (2008) Investigating the effect of mental set on insight problem solving
finding: Mental set study (three experiments): sets of non-insight problems gave no set effect on later insight problems. Sets of insight problems gave facilitation or inhibition depending on problem type. Explained by representational change plus proceduralisation.
numbers: Not read in full; sample sizes unknown.
limits: Not opened (file not retrievable). Repository abstract summary only.
agent_relevance: Earlier similar problems can help or hurt. An agent that recalls past solutions risks Einstellung.

source: Chein & Weisberg (2014) Working memory and insight in verbal problems: compound remote associates
finding: Individual-difference moderator. In compound remote associate problems rated as insightful, verbal working memory and attention control (Stroop, antisaccade) explained variation in performance. This fits a business-as-usual view against a special-process view of insight.
numbers: Abstract level: higher verbal WM and attention went with more solved insight-rated problems. Think-aloud group N=27, silent group N=26.
limits: Verbal problems, not matchstick. Insight rated by self-report. Does not test representational change directly.
agent_relevance: Restructuring still uses ordinary working memory, so keep the constraint list short and visible.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese riddles reveal limits of machine insight
finding: NazoNazo benchmark: 201 Japanese children riddles needing a representational shift. 38 frontier LLMs scored far below people. Models often produce the right candidate but do not commit to it.
numbers: Non-reasoning models mean 7.6%, reasoning models 17.6%, humans mean 52.9% (120-item subset). Pooled item-level odds ratio 2.29 (95% CI 1.99 to 2.64) for reasoning vs non-reasoning, population accuracy 9.42% vs 19.25%. GPT-5 inside the human 95% CI.
limits: Riddles with Japanese wordplay, not matchstick. Gold answer found in thought log used to count candidates.
agent_relevance: The large LLM gap is selection and stopping, not generation. Supports an explicit check candidate against the constraint list step after O4 and O6.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese riddles reveal limits of machine insight
finding: Verification failure: the model proposes a correct candidate in its thought log but gives a wrong final answer. Authors also see false insight, a confident wrong reframing.
numbers: Verification failure share of wrong answers: DeepSeek-R1-0528 30.57% (48 cases, 42 correct), Gemini 2.5 Flash Preview 5.23% (9, 29 correct), Claude Opus 4 25.00% (35, 61 correct), Grok 4 39.34% (48, 72 correct). Overall range 5.23% to 39.34%.
limits: Only four models had usable thought logs. False insight is a descriptive analogy, not a measured rate.
agent_relevance: Keep a verification gate after any reframe. Reframing too early is a risk.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese riddles reveal limits of machine insight
finding: Language of reasoning (English vs Japanese) did not reliably change accuracy. Authors say the bottleneck is restructuring and evaluating hypotheses, not surface comprehension.
numbers: Grok 4 accuracy 29.5% when reasoning in Japanese vs 48.8% in English, p=0.0071. Claude Opus 4 36.7% Japanese vs 28.7% English, p=0.356. Gemini 2.5 Flash Preview p=0.369.
limits: Language was chosen by the model, not randomized. Only one difference significant.
agent_relevance: Surface wording changes do not substitute for a change in representation.

source: dAliberti & Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Large study of Aha mid-reasoning shifts in RL-trained models. Spontaneous shifts are rare and usually hurt. Externally triggered reconsideration at high entropy helps.
numbers: 1M+ traces, three domains (cryptic crosswords as representation change, math, Rush Hour). Shifts in 6.31% of samples pooled (about 7.6% for Qwen2.5-1.5B). Accuracy 2.57% for shifted vs 16.44% for non-shifted traces, N=723,200. External trigger under high entropy: +8.41 percentage points on MATH-500, smaller gains on crosswords and Rush Hour.
limits: Mostly small open models (Qwen2.5, Llama 3.1) trained with GRPO, plus GPT-4o in some plots. Shift labelled by annotators. No frontier closed models in the main result.
agent_relevance: Strongest AI evidence for an external O6 trigger. Models do not reliably restructure alone; a scaffold that forces reconsideration when uncertain does help.

source: dAliberti & Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Formal Aha events (prior failure, a shift, and a gain at the pivot) are vanishingly rare.
numbers: Rates about 1% to 3% depending on stability thresholds (for example 1.09% to 2.99% in the Fig. 4 table).
limits: Crossword reframing is not constraint relaxation.
agent_relevance: Do not expect intrinsic insight from reflection. Build O4 and O6 into the scaffold.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese riddles reveal limits of machine insight
finding: Authors frame the LLM failure as metacognitive: generation, verification and stopping are separate, and prompted self-verification can fail without outside signals.
numbers: Verification failure range 5.23% to 39.34% of wrong answers.
limits: Four models.
agent_relevance: Add an external check (rule list, test) to any reframe step.
